2|Orteronel for Metastatic
3|Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer: A
4|Multicenter, Randomized, Open-Label Phase III
5|Trial (SWOG-1216)
6|Neeraj Agarwal, MD1; Catherine M. Tangen, DrPH2; Maha H.A. Hussain, MD3; Shilpa Gupta, MD4; Melissa Plets, MS2; Primo N. Lara, MD5;
7|Andrea L. Harzstark, MD6; Przemyslaw W. Twardowski, MD7; Channing J. Paller, MD8; Dylan Zylla, MD9; Matthew R. Zibelman, MD10;
8|Ellis Levine, MD11; Bruce J. Roth, MD12; Amir Goldkorn, MD13; Daniel A. Vaena, MD14,15; Manish Kohli, MD1,16; Tony Crispino17;
9|Nicholas J. Vogelzang, MD18; Ian M. Thompson Jr, MD19; and David I. Quinn, MD13
10|abstract
11|PURPOSE Orteronel (TAK-700) is a nonsteroidal 17,20-lyase inhibitor suppressing androgen synthesis. We
12|evaluated the clinical benefit of orteronel when added to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) in patients with
13|newly diagnosed metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer.
14|METHODS In this open-label randomized phase III study, patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate
15|cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to ADT with orteronel (300 mg oral twice daily; experimental arm) or ADT
16|with bicalutamide (50 mg oral once daily; control arm). The primary objective was the comparison of overall
17|survival (OS), targeting a 33% improvement in median survival. A stratified log-rank test with a one-sided
18|P # .022 would indicate statistical significance. Secondary end points were progression-free survival (PFS),
19|prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level at 7 months (# 0.2 v 0.2 to # 4 v . 4 ng/mL), and adverse event profile.
20|RESULTS Among 1,279 patients included in the analysis, 638 were randomly assigned to the ADT plus orteronel
21|arm and 641 to the control arm. The median age was 68 years; 49% had extensive disease. After a median
22|follow-up of 4.9 years, there was a significant improvement in PFS (median 47.6 v 23.0 months, hazard ratio
23|0.58; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.67; P , .0001) and PSA response at 7 months (P , .0001), but not in OS (median
24|81.1 v 70.2 months, hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). More grade 3/4 adverse
25|events occurred in the experimental versus the control arms (43% v 14%). Postprotocol life-prolonging therapy
26|was received by 77.4% of patients in the control arm and 61.3% of patients in the orteronel arm.
27|CONCLUSION The study did not meet the primary end point of improved OS with orteronel. The lack of correlation
28|of PFS and PSA response with OS raises concerns over assumption of their consistent surrogacy for OS in the
29|context of extensive postprotocol therapy in this setting.
30|J Clin Oncol 40:3301-3309. © 2022 by American Society of Clinical Oncology
31|INTRODUCTION
32|The cornerstone of treatment for metastatic hormone-
33|sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) is androgen depri-
34|vation therapy (ADT) with medical or surgical castra-
35|tion.1 However, disease progression universally occurs
36|on ADT, mediated by extragonadal production of an-
37|drogens or androgen-independent activation of an-
38|drogen receptor.1 The treatment paradigm of mHSPC
39|has evolved over the past decade with multiple trials
40|showing improved survival by intensification of ADT with
41|either docetaxel chemotherapy or abiraterone, which
42|inhibits a pivotal enzyme in intra- and extragonadal
43|androgen synthesis (ie, CYP17 [CYP17 hydroxylase,
44|CYP17, 20 lyase]) located in the testes and adrenal
45|glands.1-5 More recently, two direct, potent, and specific
46|inhibitors of the androgen receptor, apalutamide and
47|enzalutamide, were approved on the basis of improved
48|survival in phase III trials.1,6,7 Currently, the most
49|common sequencing of these agents in the treatment of
50|metastatic prostate cancer is abiraterone acetate fol-
51|lowed by enzalutamide or docetaxel.8 One challenge
52|with abiraterone acetate is the requirement for coad-
53|ministration of corticosteroids because of inhibition of
54|CYP17 hydroxylase.1 This results in diminished cortisol
55|production and leads to secondary mineralocorticoid
56|excess, with symptoms such as electrolyte abnormali-
57|ties, hypertension, and edema.1
58|Orteronel (TAK-700) is a novel CYP17 inhibitor. In
59|comparison with abiraterone acetate, orteronel inhibits
60|CYP17, 20 lyase with greater specificity compared with
61|CYP17 hydroxylase and does not generally lead to the
62|syndrome of secondary mineralocorticoid excess.9,10

1|We hypothesized that the addition of orteronel to ADT would
2|improve overall survival (OS), progression-free survival
3|(PFS), and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) response rela-
4|tive to bicalutamide with ADT among men with mHSPC.
5|METHODS
6|Trial Design and Conduct
7|The S1216 trial was a phase III, randomized, open-label,
8|multicenter trial involving patients with mHSPC. The trial
9|was designed by the SWOG study team and was approved
10|by the National Cancer Institute (NCI). Patients were en-
11|rolled
12|from
13|248
14|academic
15|and
16|community
17|centers
18|throughout the United States, incorporating three other
19|NCI-funded cooperative groups (ECOG-ACRIN, ALLIANCE,
20|and NRG). The NCI Central Institutional Review Board
21|approved the initial version of the Protocol (online only) and
22|all subsequent amendments. The study was conducted in
23|accordance with the International Conference on Harmo-
24|nization of Good Clinical Practice guidelines and the
25|principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Signed written
26|consent was obtained from all patients. First and last au-
27|thors (N.A. and D.I.Q.) and the statisticians (C.M.T. and
28|M.P.) among the authors assume responsibility for the
29|completeness and accuracy of the data and analyses and
30|for the fidelity of the trial to the Protocol.
31|Patients and Interventions
32|Eligible patients were required to have histologically con-
33|firmed adenocarcinoma of the prostate and metastatic
34|disease as evidenced by soft tissue and/or bony metasta-
35|ses. Enrolled patients had a Zubrod performance status of
36|0-2; a Zubrod performance status of 3 was allowed if from
37|bone pain only and a PSA $ 2.0 ng/mL. No other prior
38|systemic therapy for metastatic prostate cancer was
39|allowed (with the exception of up to 30 days of ADT for
40|metastatic disease before registration), and at least 6 months
41|must have elapsed since completion of prior neoadjuvant
42|and/or adjuvant ADT. Concomitant radiotherapy was allowed
43|only for baseline symptoms per investigator's clinical judg-
44|ment during the first 4 months of protocol treatment. Patients
45|who had not started any therapy with luteinizing hormone-
46|releasing hormone (LHRH) agonist, antagonist, or orchi-
47|ectomy (early induction group) and patients who had already
48|started therapy with LHRH agonist, antagonist, or orchi-
49|ectomy within 30 days before registration (late induction
50|group) were eligible. Patients who were deemed to have
51|extensive mHSPC were eligible for enrollment if, on the basis
52|of the judgment of the treating physician, they were un-
53|suitable candidates for docetaxel or if they declined doce-
54|taxel therapy.11
55|Exclusion criteria included brain metastases; prior therapy
56|with ketoconazole, abiraterone acetate, or enzalutamide;
57|New York Heart Association class III or IV heart failure at
58|screening or thromboembolic event; unstable angina
59|pectoris; myocardial infarction; or serious uncontrolled
60|cardiac arrhythmia # 6 months before registration.
61|Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive
62|orteronel (300 mg) orally twice daily or bicalutamide (50
63|mg) administered orally once daily, in addition to contin-
64|uous ADT. Patient assignment was dynamically balanced
65|on three stratification factors: severity of disease (minimal v
66|extensive), Zubrod performance status (0-1 v 2-3), and
67|preregistration treatment status (early v late induction).
68|Severity (or risk) of disease criteria in this study was orig-
69|inally reported in 1989, and since then, it has been used in
70|all SWOG trials in the mHSPC setting to date.11-13 Minimal
71|disease was defined as involvement of vertebrae and/or
72|pelvic bones and/or lymph nodes, and extensive disease
73|was defined as that with greater than minimal involvement.
74|Dynamic balancing is a general procedure for treatment
75|CONTEXT
76|Key Objective
77|We examined if adding orteronel, a novel androgen axis inhibitor, to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) would improve
78|outcomes compared with ADT plus bicalutamide in men with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer in a phase III
79|trial.
80|Knowledge Generated
81|Addition of orteronel to ADT resulted in a significant improvement in progression-free survival and prostate-specific antigen
82|response but not in overall survival (OS), the primary end point. Interestingly, the median OS of patients in the control arm
83|of SWOG-1216 was 24 months higher than that in patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer on the
84|SWOG-9346 trial (reported in 2013) who had similar disease severity and also received ADT plus bicalutamide (70.2 v 46
85|months).
86|Relevance
87|These results indicate that orteronel is likely not an effective androgen axis inhibitor compared with recently approved agents
88|in this setting. Higher than anticipated OS of patients in the control arm is reflective of therapeutic advancements made
89|over the past decade in men with metastatic prostate cancer.

4|End Points
5|The primary end point was OS, which was defined as the time
6|from random assignment to the date of death from any cause.
7|Secondary end points were PFS, PSA response rates, and
8|adverse events (AEs) rate. PFS was defined as the time from
9|random assignment to first documentation of PSA progression
10|($ 25% increase and an absolute increase of at least 2 ng/mL
11|from the nadir PSA), radiologic progression (two or more new
12|lesions on radionuclide bone scans, per Prostate Cancer
13|Working Group 2 [PCWG2] criteria, and/or soft tissue pro-
14|gression per RECIST version 1.1), clinical progression
15|(symptomatic deterioration) or death, whichever occurred
16|first. PSA response rates were divided into complete response
17|(CR; PSA , 0.2 ng/mL), partial response (PR; PSA between
18|0.2 and 4.0 ng/mL), and no response (NR; PSA . 4.0 ng/mL)
19|at a 7-month landmark after random assignment.
20|Assessments
21|Patients were assessed for efficacy according to the
22|modified RECIST version 1.1 with the use of computed
23|tomography or magnetic resonance imaging of the chest,
24|abdomen, and pelvis during screening (# 6 weeks be-
25|fore random assignment) and according to PCWG2
26|criteria with the use of bone scanning.15 Progression
27|events were assessed by the treating investigator.
28|Statistical Analysis
29|The median survival of patients randomly assigned to ADT
30|plus bicalutamide was assumed to be 54 months on the
31|basis of revised estimates from previous SWOG studies
32|(48 months on the basis of the median from SWOG-S9346,
33|the intermittent v continuous ADT phase III trial, and an
34|additional 6 months from the newer drug approvals in the
35|castrate-resistant setting, which may extend survival).11
36|With 2.75 years to accrue 1,186 eligible patients and an
37|additional follow-up of 3 years, we had a 90% power to
38|determine a 33% improvement in median OS from 54 to
39|72 months (one-sided a 5 .025). A final analysis was
40|prespecified after 523 deaths in the combined arms using a
41|one-sided a 5 .022 to account for interim analyses.
42|Demographic and clinical characteristics at baseline were
43|summarized with the use of descriptive statistics. The
44|primary statistical method comparing time-to-event end
45|points was a stratified log-rank test, with stratification
46|according to prespecified factors. The Kaplan-Meier
47|product-limit method was used to generate the survival
48|and PFS curves in Figures 1, 2, Appendix Figure A2
49|(online only), and the Cox proportional hazards model
50|with covariate adjustment for stratification factors was
51|used to estimate treatment hazard ratios (HRs) and as-
52|sociated CIs for survival and PFS. Homogeneity of treat-
53|ment effect was descriptively evaluated with a forest plot
54|showing the survival HR and 95% CI for each subgroup
55|defined by the stratification factors and race using a Cox
56|regression model with no covariate adjustment. The

20|Six hundred thirty-eight patients were randomly assigned to
21|the orteronel arm, and 641 were randomly assigned to the
22|control arm. At the cutoff date (February 5, 2021) for the
23|final analysis after 525 deaths (and 787 PFS events), the
24|median follow-up time was 4.9 years. Demographic and
25|clinical characteristics at baseline were well balanced
26|(Table 1). The median age of the patients for the orteronel
27|and control arms was 67.6 and 68.1 years, respectively.
28|Across both groups, approximately 10% of the patients
29|were African American, 49% had extensive disease, and
30|96% had a Zubrod performance status of 0 or 1.
31|Primary End Point
32|Analysis for OS occurred after the prespecified 525 deaths
33|were observed (251 in the orteronel group and 274 in the
34|control group). The median OS in the orteronel group was
35|81.1 months as compared with 70.2 months in the control
36|group. The OS rate at 5 years was 59.7% in the orteronel
37|group and 57.9% in the control group (HR for death 0.86;
38|95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). No statistically
39|significant improvement in OS was observed with orteronel
40|compared with control (Fig 1). This lack of treatment effect
41|on OS seemed consistent across stratification factors, in-
42|cluding disease severity, and by race (Fig 3 and Appendix
43|Table A3, online only).
44|Secondary End Points
45|Analysis of PFS occurred after 787 events were observed
46|(343 in the orteronel group and 444 in the control group).

17|DISCUSSION
18|In this study, addition of orteronel to ADT compared with
19|bicalutamide led to a statistically significant improvement in
20|PFS and PSA response. Although the approximately 11-
21|month improvement in median OS with orteronel appears
22|clinically meaningful, it did not reach the prespecified re-
23|quirement for statistical significance. The assumption of 54-
24|month OS for the control arm was a substantial underesti-
25|mate, exceeded by 16 months in the actual results, chal-
26|lenging the probability of a statistically significant result.
27|The discrepancy between improvement in PFS but not in
28|OS might have occurred because of receipt of subsequent
29|life-prolonging therapy in a large proportion of patients in
30|the control arm. The primary end point of OS evaluated not
31|only the benefit of early addition of orteronel but also the
32|impact of subsequent life-prolonging therapies including
33|abiraterone acetate, enzalutamide, docetaxel, cabazitaxel,
34|sipuleucel-T, and radium-223.16-23 In this study, 77.4% of
35|the patients who progressed in the control arm received
36|subsequent life-prolonging therapies compared with 21%-
37|64% of patients in phase III studies in this setting reported
38|since 2013 where the control arm comprised ADT only
39|without recently approved novel agents (nonintensified
40|ADT; Appendix Table A2, online only). The receipt of
41|subsequent life-prolonging therapies by the majority of
42|patients on the control arm might have also resulted in an
43|absolute median OS of 70 months, the highest ever reported
44|for patients on a nonintensified ADT control arm of con-
45|temporary trials in mHSPC. It is also possible that the results
46|from the CHAARTED trial, which reported approximately
47|1 year after activation of SWOG-1216 and showed signifi-
48|cant improvement in OS with docetaxel in patients with
49|high-volume disease, prompted a preferential recruitment
50|of patients with low-volume disease on the SWOG-1216
51|trial, leading to an unexpected improvement in the OS in
52|both arms, especially in the control arm. For example, the
53|median OS in patients with low-volume mHSPC in the
54|CHAARTED trial had not been reached after a median
55|follow-up of 53.7 months and was 83.4 months in the
56|GETUG AFU-15 trial.24,25 Nonetheless, when compared
57|with the median OS of men on the SWOG-9346 trial in the
58|mHSPC setting (reported in 2013), where all patients re-
59|ceived ADT plus bicalutamide and which had almost an
60|identical proportion of men with extensive disease by SWOG
61|criteria of disease severity (48% v 49%), the median OS in
62|the control arm of SWOG-1216 was 24 months higher (46 v
63|70.2 months) (Appendix Figure A2).11

1|SWOG-1216 is the third phaseIII trial investigating the use of
2|orteronel in the metastatic prostate cancer setting after the
3|ELM-PC5 and ELM-PC4 trials failed to meet their primary
4|end point of OS. The ELM-PC5 trial was conducted in the
5|postdocetaxel
6|metastatic
7|castration-resistant
8|prostate
9|cancer (mCRPC) setting, whereas ELM-PC4 trial was
10|conducted in the predocetaxel mCRPC setting.26,27 Re-
11|sults of these three trials, which combined and enrolled
12|more than 3000 patients with metastatic prostate cancer,
13|suggest that orteronel is likely not an effective androgen
14|axis inhibitor compared with recently approved agents
15|such as abiraterone, apalutamide, and enzalutamide.
16|Furthermore, both PFS and OS were significantly im-
17|proved with addition of abiraterone, apalutamide, and
18|enzalutamide to ADT compared with ADT alone in the
19|LATITUDE, TITAN, and the ARCHES trials, respectively,
20|all conducted in the mHSPC setting (Appendix Table A2).
21|The strengths of this study include enrollment of patients from
22|academic and community centers across the United States,
23|proportionate representation of African-American patients
24|(highest to date among all contemporary trials), and a rep-
25|resentative patient population as evident by the risk status
26|(approximately 50% high risk). These results emphasize the
27|need to account for receipt of subsequent life-prolonging
28|therapy and a need for validated surrogate intermediate
29|end points to expedite drug development in a time where the
30|treatment paradigm in the mCRPC setting is rapidly changing.
31|Given the improved OS in men with mHSPC receiving non-
32|intensified therapy, it may also be prudent to focus on de-
33|signing trials for those at the highest risk of early disease
34|progression and death. The results of SWOG-1216 indicate
35|that access to life-prolonging therapies, approved over the
36|past decade, has significantly improved outcomes in patients
37|with metastatic prostate cancer. Furthermore, this trial pro-
38|vides survival estimates in the contemporary era when pa-
39|tients with mHSPC have access to multiple approved life-
40|prolonging therapies. These contemporary survival data will
41|be invaluable for counseling of patients with newly diagnosed
42|mHSPC and for design of future clinical trials in this setting.

result.relation_rationale: The abstract reports the requested grade 3/4 adverse-event comparison (43% vs 14%) in the randomized orteronel and bicalutamide groups. The registry defines its safety endpoint as CTCAE v4.0 grade 3 through 5 events related to study drugs, among treated participants, over treatment and follow-up. The main article table also reports grade 3-5 values, but gives 13% for control, while the abstract says 14%.

METHODS In this open-label randomized phase III study, patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate
cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to ADT with orteronel (300 mg oral twice daily; experimental arm) or ADT
with bicalutamide (50 mg oral once daily; control arm). The primary objective was the comparison of overall
survival (OS), targeting a 33% improvement in median survival. A stratified log-rank test with a one-sided
P # .022 would indicate statistical significance. Secondary end points were progression-free survival (PFS),
prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level at 7 months (# 0.2 v 0.2 to # 4 v . 4 ng/mL), and adverse event profile.
RESULTS Among 1,279 patients included in the analysis, 638 were randomly assigned to the ADT plus orteronel
arm and 641 to the control arm. The median age was 68 years; 49% had extensive disease. After a median
follow-up of 4.9 years, there was a significant improvement in PFS (median 47.6 v 23.0 months, hazard ratio
0.58; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.67; P , .0001) and PSA response at 7 months (P , .0001), but not in OS (median
81.1 v 70.2 months, hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). More grade 3/4 adverse
events occurred in the experimental versus the control arms (43% v 14%). Postprotocol life-prolonging therapy
was received by 77.4% of patients in the control arm and 61.3% of patients in the orteronel arm.

Prostate cancer is the most common non-cutaneous malignancy among American men. (1)

result.relation_rationale: The abstract reports the requested grade 3/4 adverse-event comparison (43% vs 14%) in the randomized orteronel and bicalutamide groups. METHODS In this open-label randomized phase III study, patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate
cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to ADT with orteronel (300 mg oral twice daily; experimental arm) or ADT
with bicalutamide (50 mg oral once daily; control arm). The primary objective was the comparison of overall
survival (OS), targeting a 33% improvement in median survival. A stratified log-rank test with a one-sided
P # .022 would indicate statistical significance. Secondary end points were progression-free survival (PFS),
prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level at 7 months (# 0.2 v 0.2 to # 4 v . 4 ng/mL), and adverse event profile.
RESULTS Among 1,279 patients included in the analysis, 638 were randomly assigned to the ADT plus orteronel
arm and 641 to the control arm. The median age was 68 years; 49% had extensive disease. After a median
follow-up of 4.9 years, there was a significant improvement in PFS (median 47.6 v 23.0 months, hazard ratio
0.58; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.67; P , .0001) and PSA response at 7 months (P , .0001), but not in OS (median
81.1 v 70.2 months, hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). More grade 3/4 adverse
events occurred in the experimental versus the control arms (43% v 14%). Postprotocol life-prolonging therapy
was received by 77.4% of patients in the control arm and 61.3% of patients in the orteronel arm.

evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

protocol documents. Search for concrete study wording such as the outcome
status, withdrawal or loss-to-follow-up labels, and the reported time point;
`missing outcome data` alone may not occur in the report. Widen the Source
scope or continue a cached cursor only as needed, and stop when comparable
observed counts or complete follow-up accounting are inspected. If the
captured Sources and bounded page windows do not establish availability,
document that limit instead of treating an empty Source group or a no-hit
search as evidence of missing outcomes.

## Reconcile availability

Keep these quantities distinct for each arm and time point:

- randomized participants;
- participants with the outcome observed;
- participants included in the reported analysis;
- participants whose outcomes were imputed; and
- post-randomization exclusions; and
- outcome events, which are a numerator rather than an observed-participant count.

An analyzed count is not necessarily an observed count. Imputed outcomes count
as missing outcome data for RoB 2. Treatment discontinuation is not missing
outcome data when follow-up and outcome ascertainment continued.

If some outcomes are missing, assess whether data remain available for nearly
all randomized participants. Keep the randomized denominator, outcome-observed
count, analyzed count, imputed count, excluded count, and event count separate
for the same arm, population, unit, and time point. Consider whether the
missing outcomes could make an important difference to this Result. For
dichotomous outcomes, compare the missing count with observed events, not only
the randomized denominator. A count below the randomized total does not settle
that question, and no universal percentage threshold replaces this impact
judgment.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring
caused by missing follow-up before the outcome could be observed. Treatment
discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that
outcome observation stopped. For time-to-event Results, censoring may still
create missing outcome information; assess its timing, reason, actual follow-up
pathway, and relation to treatment or prognosis instead of treating every
censored participant as either fully observed or missing by default.

Question 3.1 may include compact `missing_data` rows. Give each row a comparable
arm, population, unit, and time point. Use a row-level `basis` only to narrow or
add to the answer's Evidence. The server calculates differences and fractions
only after scopes match and preserves conflicting reports without choosing the
scientific answer.

When a count comparison would help before answering, call `get_domain_context`
with `missing_data` rows. Every preview row needs a nonempty `basis` containing
current-Trial Evidence references: no answer exists to supply inherited Evidence.
Inspect `comparison_cards[].missing_data`
for differences, fractions, and conflicting reports. The preview changes no
checkpoint or State revision. To retain the chosen rows, submit them with the
3.1 answer in `validate_domain_assessment`; omit row `basis` there only to reuse
the answer's Evidence when it supports those counts. After its receipt, save
the exact draft with `save_domain_judgment`.

Check each input against its source passage before using the arithmetic. The
helper subtracts supplied observed counts from randomized counts; it does not
extract counts or sum grouped departures. Keep unknown observed counts unknown.
Skip the preview when an explicit ascertainment statement resolves availability
without arithmetic.

When a row includes typed `semantics`, treat it as scope metadata, not as a
shortcut to a signalling answer. `event_count` is an event numerator and never
means that every participant's outcome was observed. `analyzed`, `safety`, and
`per_protocol` roles are denominators or populations, not availability. Keep
administrative censoring, loss to follow-up, treatment change, imputation, and
post-randomization exclusions as distinct facts. The server preserves these
fields and only derives `randomized - observed`; it does not decide whether a
censored participant is informative.

## Assess bias from missingness

If data were not available for all or nearly all participants, ask in sequence:

1. Does a bias-correcting method or informative sensitivity analysis show that
   the Result was not biased?
2. Could missingness depend on the true outcome, based on reasons, health
   status, withdrawal, loss to follow-up, or censoring?
3. If it could, is that dependence likely given arm differences, reasons,
   prognostic factors, or trial circumstances?

Simple imputation, including last observation carried forward or multiple
imputation based only on intervention group, does not by itself show freedom from
bias. A comparison that changes group attribution, such as ITT versus
as-treated, does not test unobserved outcome values unless the source establishes
that relationship. A reassuring sensitivity analysis must vary plausible
unobserved outcomes under the missingness mechanism relevant to the approved
Result. Documented reasons support reassurance only when they address the
outcome relationship.

Keep possible dependence in 3.3 separate from likely dependence in 3.4. For
3.4, state which reasons or trial circumstances support the likelihood judgment.
Absent contrary evidence alone does not establish likely dependence. Preserve
`no_information` when the card's uncertainty rule applies, even when that answer
leads to High risk of bias.

D3.2 does not allow `no_information`. When no bias-correcting evidence is found,
use the question card to choose a permitted negative or probably-negative answer
with the appropriate limitation or Evidence basis. Do not fabricate direct
support for the absence of bias.

## Paired premise check

Use neutral pairs to keep the seams separate: complete outcome ascertainment
versus an analysis denominator with unresolved availability; common administrative
censoring versus follow-up stopping after worsening symptoms. The changed premise
is the ascertainment or missingness mechanism, not a percentage threshold. The
pair supplies no answer or risk label; the host still grounds each proposition
in exact Evidence and retains No information or High where the official path
requires it.

METHODS In this open-label randomized phase III study, patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate
cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to ADT with orteronel (300 mg oral twice daily; experimental arm) or ADT
with bicalutamide (50 mg oral once daily; control arm). The primary objective was the comparison of overall
survival (OS), targeting a 33% improvement in median survival. A stratified log-rank test with a one-sided
P # .022 would indicate statistical significance. Secondary end points were progression-free survival (PFS),
prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level at 7 months (# 0.2 v 0.2 to # 4 v . 4 ng/mL), and adverse event profile.
RESULTS Among 1,279 patients included in the analysis, 638 were randomly assigned to the ADT plus orteronel
arm and 641 to the control arm. The median age was 68 years; 49% had extensive disease. After a median
follow-up of 4.9 years, there was a significant improvement in PFS (median 47.6 v 23.0 months, hazard ratio
0.58; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.67; P , .0001) and PSA response at 7 months (P , .0001), but not in OS (median
81.1 v 70.2 months, hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). More grade 3/4 adverse
events occurred in the experimental versus the control arms (43% v 14%). Postprotocol life-prolonging therapy
was received by 77.4% of patients in the control arm and 61.3% of patients in the orteronel arm.

questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

answers.justification: The CONSORT figure reports 653 randomized to orteronel and 660 to bicalutamide. The registry reports 627 and 629 treated participants evaluable for AEs. Thus AE data were reported for about 96% of those randomized (shortfalls of 26 and 31). Given the small, similar shortfalls and the large reported difference in severe-AE rates, the missing outcomes are unlikely to make an important difference to this result. This is a probable judgment because individual AE status for those not evaluated is unavailable.
unknowns: The individual AE status and detailed reason for non-evaluability of all 57 randomized participants are not reported.

counterevidence.implication: Outcome data were not reported for every randomized participant; the small shortfall still requires an impact judgment.

questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the method is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the instrument has demonstrated poor validity. response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.

considerations: Possible influence without evidence it occurred maps differently from likely influence.

METHODS In this open-label randomized phase III study, patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate
cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to ADT with orteronel (300 mg oral twice daily; experimental arm) or ADT
with bicalutamide (50 mg oral once daily; control arm). The primary objective was the comparison of overall
survival (OS), targeting a 33% improvement in median survival. A stratified log-rank test with a one-sided
P # .022 would indicate statistical significance. Secondary end points were progression-free survival (PFS),
prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level at 7 months (# 0.2 v 0.2 to # 4 v . 4 ng/mL), and adverse event profile.
RESULTS Among 1,279 patients included in the analysis, 638 were randomly assigned to the ADT plus orteronel
arm and 641 to the control arm. The median age was 68 years; 49% had extensive disease. After a median
follow-up of 4.9 years, there was a significant improvement in PFS (median 47.6 v 23.0 months, hazard ratio
0.58; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.67; P , .0001) and PSA response at 7 months (P , .0001), but not in OS (median
81.1 v 70.2 months, hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). More grade 3/4 adverse
events occurred in the experimental versus the control arms (43% v 14%). Postprotocol life-prolonging therapy
was received by 77.4% of patients in the control arm and 61.3% of patients in the orteronel arm.

c.
Criteria for Discontinuation of TAK-700

If for any reason, TAK-700 has been held for > 60 days, it will be permanently
discontinued, but patient can remain on protocol treatment just receiving LHRH
agonist.

d.
Hypertension

Decisions to hold, decrease and re-escalate TAK-700 are based on three factors.
The first is whether the treating physician considers hypertension to be related to
TAK-700. The second is to assess the grade of the hypertension. The third is
persistence of blood pressure (BP) readings (and not an isolated BP reading).

Modification of TAK-700 dose should be performed only if hypertension is
considered related to TAK-700. Grading of hypertension should be based on
persistent BP readings (and NOT based on how many antihypertensive drugs
patient is on, as mentioned in the CTCAE v4 grading guidelines). For example, if
a patient is on ≥ 1 antihypertensive medication this would suggest a CTCAE v4
Grade 3 hypertension, however, if the BP reading is 120/87, it should be graded
as Grade 1 for treatment decision and dose modification under this protocol.
Finally, BP readings used to grade hypertension should be based on more than
one BP reading taken at least one hour apart and not based on an isolated BP
reading.

answers.justification: AEs were graded using CTCAE v4.0, a standardized toxicity grading system. The protocol also specified repeated blood-pressure readings for hypertension grading, supporting a defined assessment method. No evidence indicates that the method was invalid or insensitive to grade 3/4 toxicity.

The protocol scheduled AE forms monthly for the first four months and then every three months while participants remained on protocol treatment, with a final AE form at discontinuation. It specifies only PSA and follow-up forms after treatment ended. The article reports substantially different median PFS by group (47.6 vs 23.0 months), suggesting that time on treatment and therefore the opportunity to record AEs could differ. The scheduled method was shared, but ascertainment stopped with protocol treatment; this creates a plausible differential opportunity over the broad approved window.
unknowns: The article does not report arm-specific treatment exposure duration or post-treatment AE ascertainment, so the magnitude of any differential detection opportunity is unknown.

counterevidence.implication: The protocol used the same scheduled AE reporting cadence in both arms while on treatment.

questions.decision_rule: Compare the approved Result with the applicable plan for the exact intervention comparison, cohort, endpoint, time window, population, analysis, and effect measure. Distinguish source creation/version and amendment dates from trial events and retrieval time; only compare chronology when the relevant events and precision are established. Changes made before unblinded data were available, or clearly unrelated to results such as a broken machine, do not raise concerns.
evidence_needed: A sufficiently detailed protocol or SAP, its source-located chronology and finalization date relative to unblinded outcome data, and the reported analysis.

For an original plan and an amended plan, capture the source-located content and chronology separately. An embedded SAP can be applicable evidence when its comparison, cohort, and Result fields match; an absent or unresolved plan remains an information limit.
questions.no_information_rule: Use a definitive answer when firm evidence establishes timing and correspondence. Use a probable answer when source facts and trial circumstances support only an inference. Use no_information when neither is supported. A plan mention or matching endpoint alone does not establish timing.

answer_anchors.text: The result follows a sufficiently detailed plan finalized before unblinded outcome data were available.
The result did not follow such a pre-specified plan.
Analysis intentions or their timing are not sufficiently reported.

considerations: Assess correspondence between the applicable plan and the exact approved Result: outcome, time point, population, effect measure, and analysis must be compared.

Assess applicability before chronology: a platform or master plan may cover several comparisons and cohorts, so its presence does not establish applicability to the approved Result. Establish chronology separately: plan finalization must precede availability of unblinded outcome data; a source creation date, registry posting or update date, amendment date, or retrieval date is not automatically the relevant trial chronology.

Current registry content does not establish unseen historical intent, and a data cutoff is not investigator unblinding. Preserve unresolved applicability or chronology instead of filling the gap from report wording that merely looks prespecified.

Results-driven selection is a separate concern from whether a plan exists or whether its chronology is known. Do not infer selection merely from an amendment or from a mismatch without evidence that the choice was driven by results.

Neutral paired control: an applicable plan for the approved cohort differs from a platform plan for another phase; pre-unblinding finalization differs from ambiguous chronology only in the timing premise.

current registry content treated as historical intent
a data cutoff treated as investigator unblinding

questions.bias_construct: Whether the result was selected from multiple eligible analyses of the data on the basis of results.
considerations: Use the review's prespecified outcome-domain eligibility criteria, not only the reported Result, and compare the reported analysis with the complete set of multiple eligible analyses. Keep the exact Result's comparison, cohort, endpoint, time window, population, and effect measure fixed.

An applicable plan's correspondence and chronology are distinct checks. The approved Result fixes the target being assessed; it does not erase eligible alternative analyses or turn an unresolved alternative into an observed selection.
Reporting several analyses together establishes multiplicity, not result-based selection. Inability to rule out selection does not establish that it probably occurred.

When the plan is insufficiently detailed and multiple eligible analyses remain possible but unresolved, use no_information; do not turn an unobserved selection into no/probably no merely because the report names one analysis. Preserve the evidence path's support for Low, Some concerns, High, or legitimate uncertainty without forcing a severity category.
questions.decision_rule: Multiplicity alone does not establish result-based selection. Answer yes or probably yes only when the justification identifies the eligible alternatives, the reporting or selection evidence, and why selection likely depended on the results. Answer no or probably no when all eligible intended analyses are reported, only one possible analysis exists, or an unrelated inconsistency is explained.
evidence_needed: The protocol or SAP's eligible analysis methods and which were reported, including adjustment, transformation, composite definitions, and missing-data strategies.
invalid_shortcuts: a registry link without analysis detail
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when intentions are unavailable or insufficiently detailed and more than one eligible analysis was possible.
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ if there is clear evidence that a measurement was analysed in multiple eligible ways, but data for only one or a subset of analyses is fully reported without justification, and the fully reported result is likely to have been selected on the basis of the results. Answer ‘No information’ if analysis intentions are not available or are not reported in sufficient detail and there is more than one way in which the outcome measurement could have been analysed.

METHODS In this open-label randomized phase III study, patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate
cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to ADT with orteronel (300 mg oral twice daily; experimental arm) or ADT
with bicalutamide (50 mg oral once daily; control arm). The primary objective was the comparison of overall
survival (OS), targeting a 33% improvement in median survival. A stratified log-rank test with a one-sided
P # .022 would indicate statistical significance. Secondary end points were progression-free survival (PFS),
prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level at 7 months (# 0.2 v 0.2 to # 4 v . 4 ng/mL), and adverse event profile.
RESULTS Among 1,279 patients included in the analysis, 638 were randomly assigned to the ADT plus orteronel
arm and 641 to the control arm. The median age was 68 years; 49% had extensive disease. After a median
follow-up of 4.9 years, there was a significant improvement in PFS (median 47.6 v 23.0 months, hazard ratio
0.58; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.67; P , .0001) and PSA response at 7 months (P , .0001), but not in OS (median
81.1 v 70.2 months, hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). More grade 3/4 adverse
events occurred in the experimental versus the control arms (43% v 14%). Postprotocol life-prolonging therapy
was received by 77.4% of patients in the control arm and 61.3% of patients in the orteronel arm.

8.1
NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events

This study will utilize the CTCAE (NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events)
Version 4.0 for toxicity and Serious Adverse Event reporting. A copy of the CTCAE
Version 4.0 can be downloaded from the CTEP home page (http://ctep.cancer.gov). All
appropriate treatment areas should have access to a copy of the CTCAE Version 4.0.

Note: The above refers to adverse events considered at least possibly
related to TAK-700. Reassess the AE after 2 weeks or sooner if the AE
worsens. Continue to reassess periodically (per investigator's clinical
judgement) until the event is resolved or stabilized. Continue to adjust
the TAK-700 dose until the dose is optimally titrated. During dose
escalation, if toxicities that are at least possibly related to TAK-700
recur, TAK-700 can be continued at Level -1 or Level -2 without full
dose escalation per investigator's clinical judgment.


c.
Criteria for Discontinuation of TAK-700

If for any reason, TAK-700 has been held for > 60 days, it will be permanently
discontinued, but patient can remain on protocol treatment just receiving LHRH
agonist.

d.
Hypertension

Decisions to hold, decrease and re-escalate TAK-700 are based on three factors.
The first is whether the treating physician considers hypertension to be related to
TAK-700. The second is to assess the grade of the hypertension. The third is
persistence of blood pressure (BP) readings (and not an isolated BP reading).

Modification of TAK-700 dose should be performed only if hypertension is
considered related to TAK-700. Grading of hypertension should be based on
persistent BP readings (and NOT based on how many antihypertensive drugs
patient is on, as mentioned in the CTCAE v4 grading guidelines). For example, if
a patient is on ≥ 1 antihypertensive medication this would suggest a CTCAE v4
Grade 3 hypertension, however, if the BP reading is 120/87, it should be graded
as Grade 1 for treatment decision and dose modification under this protocol.
Finally, BP readings used to grade hypertension should be based on more than
one BP reading taken at least one hour apart and not based on an isolated BP
reading.

answers.warrant: AEs were graded using CTCAE v4.0, a standardized toxicity grading system. The protocol also specified repeated blood-pressure readings for hypertension grading, supporting a defined assessment method. No evidence indicates that the method was invalid or insensitive to grade 3/4 toxicity.

| RoB 2 domain | Judgment |
|---|---|
| Randomization process | Some concerns |

The eTable’s statement that the toxicity definition was unreported is qualified by the registry, which specifies related Grade 3–5 AEs using CTCAE v4.0. However, the report gives differing descriptions of the endpoint: the abstract reports Grade 3/4 AEs (43% vs 14%), while Table 2 reports Grade 3–5 AEs (43% vs 13%). The measurement concern also reflects the possibility of unequal AE observation time: collection was tied to treatment, and median progression-free survival differed between groups. That concern is an inference from the reported follow-up procedures and treatment duration, rather than direct evidence of differential ascertainment.
